title: Commit Elasticity & Rollover Playbook: modeling lead-time and utilization impacts for reserved GPU pools
content:
Purpose
This is a working playbook for modeling the economics of reserved GPU pool commitments when customers have the ability to: move commitments between quarters, roll unused hours forward, or partially scale down before term end. Focus is on three levers we don't model well today: lead-time for commit changes, rollover credit mechanics, and effective commit elasticity (how much committed capacity customers actually use).

Audience
- Product and pricing (primary)
- Go-to-market and sales engineering (input on negotiation behavior)
- Finance (NRC/ARR recognition implications)
- Solutions/Professional services (implementation lead times)

Context / Motivation
We have many existing analyses that assume a static committed GPU-months number for a contract. In the real world customers frequently: reduce consumption late in quarter, request to shift committed capacity between regions, ask for rollover of unused months, or negotiate mid-term reductions in exchange for extended term or price concessions. These behaviors change the realized utilization and therefore unit economics of Dedicated. This doc captures experimental spreadsheet logic, candidate policy options (rollover vs credit vs forgiveness), and draft recommendations for sales and billing integration.

High-level assumptions used in the model
- Commit unit: GPU-month (one GPU, fully allocated for 30 days). Pricing is per GPU-month.
- Baseline cloud cost (amortized infra cost per GPU-month): $2,400 (post-commit discount we pay).
- List price to customer (committed): $4,000/GPU-month (example blended tier).
- On-demand equivalent: $5,500/GPU-month.
- Typical lead time to reconfigure dedicated pool (region/size): 3-6 weeks. Minimum billable notice: Tbd in policy.
- Rollover options considered: full-month rollover credits, 50% credit, or expiration.
- Elasticity parameter e in [0..1]: e=0 => committed never shifts; e=1 => customer uses 0 of committed capacity (extreme). We use a more sensible range 0.05–0.30 in experiments.

Model structure (spreadsheet tabs / inputs described)
- Inputs: contract_term_months, committed_gpus, baseline_cloud_cost_per_gpu_mo, committed_price_per_gpu_mo, on_demand_price_per_gpu_mo, average_utilization_pct, elasticity_factor_e, rollover_policy (full/partial/none), lead_time_weeks, churn_probability
- Derived: provisioned_cost = committed_gpus * baseline_cloud_cost_per_gpu_mo
- Realized_usage = committed_gpus * average_utilization_pct * (1 - elasticity_factor_e)
- Effective_unit_cost_realized = provisioned_cost / max(Realized_usage, 1)  (guard against division by zero)
- Revenue = committed_gpus * committed_price_per_gpu_mo * contract_term_months - credits_paid_for_rollover
- Margin = Revenue - provisioned_cost * contract_term_months - expected_overage_cloud_costs + surcharge_recoveries

Quick example run (numbers inline so easier to sanity-check)
Inputs (example customer):
- term = 12 months
- committed = 40 GPUs
- baseline_cloud_cost = 2400 / GPU-month
- committed_price = 4000 / GPU-month
- avg_utilization = 0.75 (75% of committed pool actively used)
- elasticity e = 0.12 (12% of committed capacity effectively not used due to customer behavior)
- rollover policy = 50% credit for unused months
- lead_time_weeks = 4

Derived numbers:
- provisioned_cost_monthly = 40 * 2400 = $96,000
- expected_realized_usage_monthly = 40 * 0.75 * (1 - 0.12) = 40 * 0.75 * 0.88 = 26.4 GPU-months used (this intentionally treats utilization pct as fraction of the pool that could be active; we could instead model active v. idle GPUs differently)
- effective_cost_per_used_gpu = 96,000 / 26.4 = ~$3,636 per used GPU-month (this is the true economic cost if we assume unused committed capacity has zero salvage value)
- monthly_revenue = 40 * 4000 = $160,000
- monthly_margin_before_rollover = 160k - 96k = $64,000
- if rollover credits paid (50% of unused capacity at committed price): unused = 40 - 40*0.75*(1-0.12)/40 = this is messy in prose; explicit: unused_gpu_months = committed - (committed * avg_util * (1-e)) = 40 - 26.4 = 13.6; credit_cost = 13.6 * 4000 * 0.5 = $27,200; margin_after_rollover = 64k - 27.2k = $36,800

Observations from quick run:
- Even with a fairly high list margin (40%), realized economic margin can be compressed heavily if utilization is lower than expected and rollover credits are generous.
- The elasticity parameter has non-linear effects when utilization is already low. If utilization drops below ~50% the effective per-used-unit economics approach on-demand levels.

Sensitivity experiments to run (spreadsheet tab: sensitivity-grid)
- Sweep avg_util from 0.45 to 0.95 by 0.05 increments.
- Sweep elasticity e from 0.0 to 0.30 by 0.02 increments.
- For each combo, compute: effective_cost_per_used_gpu, margin_pct, break-even committed price (price where margin = 0).
- Additional dimension: rollover_policy in {none, 25pct, 50pct, full}.
- Additional dimension: lead_time_weeks in {2,4,8} to capture ability to reallocate pool (shorter lead-time reduces risk).

Policy levers and salesperson tradeoffs (notes for SRE/product to discuss)
- Rollover credits: full rollover increases sale conversion but transfers utilization risk to Redwood. Partial rollover (25–50%) is a good compromise.
- Lead time SLAs: offering a guaranteed 2-week reconfigure window as a paid managed option (premium) could reduce our unit risk. But operationally expensive.
- Convert cold capacity to a short-term on-demand marketplace when idle (internal placement between customers) — requires billing/provisioning automation.
- Minimum notice windows and penalty tiers: e.g., reductions requested with <6 weeks notice trigger a 50% reduction in rebate/rollover credit.
- Incentive trade: allow rollover if customer increases future commit by X% (rollover as an acquisition credit).

Spreadsheet layout suggestions (tab-by-tab)
- Readme: short description, owner, last run date, how to use
- Inputs: single cell parameters with guarded validation (data validation dropdowns for policies)
- Scenarios: named scenarios for sales use (Conservative, Baseline, Aggressive, ChurnHeavy)
- Sensitivity-grid: big matrix output + heatmap conditional formatting (margin % color)
- Waterfall: revenue -> provisioned costs -> credits -> overage -> margin -> break-even price
- Negotiation-playbook: recommended concession ladders (e.g., 10% price concession => required 15% increase in commit term)

Negotiation playbook (practical rules for AE/SE)
- If prospect requests full-month rollover: require 12-month minimum AND a 10% price uplift OR require 90-day minimum notice to use rollover.
- If prospect requests 100% regional mobility (move pool between regions mid-term): charge a relocation fee equal to 1 month of committed price per 10 GPUs moved for <6 weeks notice.
- Short-notice downsizes (<6 weeks): allow one 10% reduction per year without penalty. Anything additional — rollover credit reduced to 25% or a termination fee.

Edge cases and modeling caveats (we need to decide policy, not model):
- Seasonal customers: model month-by-month expected utilization profile rather than constant avg_util number. For many customers (retail, edtech), utilization has strong seasonality and rollover policies interact badly.
- Multi-region mapping: re-assignment costs and cross-region price differentials need to be accounted for. If we repurpose idle GPUs to different region customers, the realized cost changes.
- Accounting impacts: rollover credits may impact revenue recognition and rebate accruals. Need finance to sign off on allowed credit offsets and how to book deferred revenue.

Questions to resolve (TODOs)
- What is legal/billing tolerance for negative reconciliations? (Claire to check with Finance/Legal)
- Can SRE automate pool reassignments within 2-week windows? (Ethan to prototype with infra team)
- What on-demand marketplace latency and SLAs are reasonable to convert idle capacity? (product ops)
- How do renewals change elasticity? Historically, existing customers are more stable — can we rely on lower e for renewals? (pull cohort data)

Data tasks / validation (data science + finance)
- Extract historical dedicated pool utilization logs for last 24 months (group by customer, region, contract). Compute realized_util_pct and frequency of mid-term changes.
- Estimate elasticity by observing utilization drift in the 3 months following a commit signing vs baseline.
- Run bootstrapped sensitivity to get 95% CI on predicted margin under existing rollovers.

Draft recommendations (opinionated, for leadership)
1) Move to a partial-rollover default: 25% of unused committed GPU-months, unless customer pays a 10% price premium, then full rollover. Rationale: balances sales flexibility and shifts some risk back to customer.
2) Implement a minimum 6-week notice rule for downsizes to qualify for any rollover credit; if notice <6 weeks, rollover credit halved. This reduces short-term churn risk and gives ops runway.
3) Invest in a small automation feature: 'pool reassigner' that can move GPUs between customers within 2 weeks. Build API + billing hook. This reduces effective elasticity and is a high-ROI engineering task.
4) Add a ‘managed fast reconfigure’ add-on priced at +15% to committed price for customers requiring guaranteed 2-week reconfigure windows.

Next steps + owners
- Data pull: Product-Analytics to run cohort utilization and elasticity estimate by 2026-03-15 (Miguel)
- Legal/Billing: confirm accounting treatment for rollover credits by 2026-03-01 (Claire)
- Infra prototype: PoC to reassign idle GPUs within 2 weeks (Ethan + infra) due 2026-04-01
- Pricing update: Draft new pricing sheet and negotiation ladders for pilot customers (Asha) due 2026-03-10

Appendix: quick CSV-style sample rows (for direct paste into spreadsheet)
scenario,term_mos,committed_gpus,avg_util,e,rollover_pct,lead_time_wks,monthly_cost,monthly_revenue,monthly_margin
baseline,12,40,0.75,0.12,0.5,4,96000,160000,64000
conservative,12,40,0.6,0.18,0.5,6,96000,160000,24000
aggressive,24,80,0.9,0.05,0.25,2,192000,320000,128000
churn-heavy,12,20,0.5,0.25,1.0,8,48000,80000,32000

Notes on uniqueness
This doc intentionally centers on the time dimension and operational lead times (notice windows, reconfigure time) as the primary driver of realized economics — a perspective we haven't prioritized in prior reserved-capacity analyses. It also ties in actionable policy recommendations (notice windows, partial rollover defaults, paid fast reconfigure) that are implementable with relatively small infra and billing investments.

If you want I can:
- convert this playbook into a one-page cheat sheet for sales with the scenario table + negotiation bullets, or
- create a live Google Sheet version with the sensitivity grid and dropdowns for rollover policy/lead time.

-- Asha
